title: The Mystery of the Tinkling Locket
markdown:
Leo was asleep, breath a small tide against the pillow, when Teddy Patch opened one button eye and decided the quiet had gone on long enough to be interesting.

“Too quiet, Comet,” he murmured. The stitched smile did not apologise for itself. “Almost too quiet.”

Comet the squirrel stood on the moonlit sill, whiskers working. The dark always unsettled him; it made the room’s familiar corners look like places that had not agreed to stay. “The squirrels were chattering about a bell. In the old beech woods. Made my fur prickle.”

“A bell,” Patch said, as if tasting the word. “Old Man Willow mentioned it.”

Comet’s tail went up like a flag in a gale. “A warning bell.”

“That,” said Patch, already a sturdy shape against the window, “is precisely what we’re going to discover.”

They were out in a flash: a dash down the rose trellis, a landing on grass still holding the day’s heat in its roots. The beech woods waited, all shadow and the taste of damp earth. Comet kept close enough that Patch could feel the tick of him.

A tiny bespectacled nose popped from the ground.

“Halt,” squeaked Bartholomew Mole, sharp as a dry twig. “Are we registered for nocturnal perambulation? Article Seven, Subsection B, clearly states—”

Patch blinked. “Just exploring. For a bell.”

“Ah. Exploration is a valid subset.” Bartholomew polished his spectacles on a scrap of moss. “Investigation, however, requires prior council registration. And a bell? Curious absence. Point of no further relevance.” He vanished, leaving only the smell of soil, which is a mole’s idea of a signature.

“Onwards,” Patch said.

Deeper in, the chatter thickened. Squirrels darted until the trees seemed to vibrate. Comet whispered, fur on end, “It’s the bell. It’s making them frantic.” In his head the clang was already enormous, a signal that meant run, hide, never have come.

A twig snapped.

Comet froze. Cold moved into his paws. His eyes shut of their own accord. Hide. Go back to Leo’s room. The trellis. The sill. The dark that at least had wallpaper.

“Don’t worry,” Patch said, a calm stone in a moving stream. “Probably a badger. Or a very enthusiastic hedgehog.” He did not hurry the next thought. “Remember our quietest idea.”

Comet’s eyes opened. Patch was still there, which was the whole of the idea.

Then Patch saw it: something tarnished in the roots of a great beech, catching moonlight the way a coin catches a wish. Not a bell. A locket shaped like one. A breeze moved, and it tinkled — a small, private sound, more sigh than warning. The squirrels were not frantic. They were curious, their chatter a baffled hum around an object that refused to be loud.

Patch nudged it. Cool. Smooth. “They’re just wondering,” he said. “Not a warning, Comet. A lost treasure.”

Comet looked at the locket, then at the squirrels. The last of the dark’s chill went out of him in a rush that surprised him more than the snap of the twig had. He had been bracing for a danger that had not bothered to exist.

He flicked his tail, once, as if testing whether it still belonged to him. “We should put it somewhere safe.”

He gathered moss, quick now, the movements of a squirrel who has decided the night is allowed to be ordinary. Patch set the locket on the small green bed. The breeze found it again. The tinkle went into the leaves and came back smaller, which was as close as a woods gets to thank you.

Dawn put rose and gold through the beeches. They climbed the trellis with less dash and more care, which is what bravery looks like on the way home. Moonlight left the sill. Comet curled against Patch’s worn side, tail content, and did not mention warning bells. The locket stayed in the roots, tinkling when it chose, and the quiet in Leo’s room went back to being only quiet.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
